title: The Editor Has Read-Only Access: Correctness Signals in Diffusion Language Models

paper.title: The Editor Has Read-Only Access: Correctness Signals in Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion language models generate code by repeatedly updating a partially masked sequence. We ask whether their internal activations encode code correctness and whether that information can improve generation. Across six diffusion models, linear probes distinguish passing from failing attempts, with the strongest reads generally appearing beyond the early layers. Controls using small semantic mutations support a connection to correctness rather than surface style alone. In comparisons with model confidence, probe point estimates offer no consistent advantage. Adding a probe-derived direction to the residual stream does not yield a dependable improvement in the tested steering settings, while the opposite direction degrades performance. We distinguish these observations from claims about statistical significance or a general inability to steer. Supplementary methods, archived results, and code document the tested interventions and the limits of their statistical calibration and reproducibility.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A model can contain information that its output does not make useful. For code generation, the distinction is concrete: an activation may help predict whether a program will pass its tests without providing an intervention that repairs the program. Work on language-model self-evaluation shows that models can sometimes estimate whether their answers are correct, although calibration depends on the task and prompting. 1 This motivates a separate question about internal representations: does a readable correctness signal also provide a way to improve generation? Diffusion language models offer a useful setting for this question. Instead of committing to one token at a time, they revise positions in a partially masked sequence over several denoising steps. A correctness-related representation could therefore appear while the program can still change. That possibility does not guarantee control. A probe can correlate with an outcome because it reads the consequences of a computation; moving the representation along the probe direction need not reproduce the computation that caused a correct answer. We study three questions in frozen code models. First, can a linear probe distinguish correct and incorrect attempts at the same programming problem? Second, does it add information beyond the model’s own confidence? Third, can a direction fitted to correctness labels improve the generated code when added to the model’s activations? We compare six diffusion models, run additional checks on DiffuCoder-7B, and use autoregressive models as a comparison rather than as a controlled test of architecture alone. The results separate readability from intervention. Correctness is readable in the tested diffusion models, but the matched confidence comparisons do not show a consistent point-estimate advantage for the probe. The tested steering procedures also do not provide a dependable improvement. These are bounded empirical observations: the captures differ across experiments, some statistical routines need recalibration, and the available code does not constitute a fully frozen reproduction environment. We retain those limits in the main interpretation and give the implementation details in the appendix.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion and language generation
sections.text: Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues introduced generative modelling through a forward process that gradually corrupts data and a learned reverse process that reconstructs it. 2 Ho and colleagues developed the denoising diffusion probabilistic model formulation that became widely used for continuous data. 3 Language requires a treatment of discrete tokens. Hoogeboom and colleagues developed multinomial diffusion for categorical data, including text. 4 Austin and colleagues studied structured discrete diffusion processes, including transitions involving an absorbing state. 5 Masked language diffusion uses this idea to generate by repeatedly predicting and updating masked positions. Diffusion-LM used continuous word-vector denoising and gradient-based guidance for controllable text generation. 6 For discrete tokens, Sahoo and colleagues developed a masked diffusion language-model objective and sampling recipe. 7 LLaDA demonstrated large-scale language modelling with a masked diffusion objective. 8 DiffuCoder adapted masked diffusion to code and studied how its generation order and reinforcement-learning procedure affect code synthesis. 9 Our experiments use these models as frozen systems. We do not train a new diffusion model or evaluate whether diffusion is generally superior to autoregressive generation. The relevant property is that internal states can be inspected and edited while multiple output positions remain revisable.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reading representations and changing behaviour
sections.text: Linear probes test whether a representation makes a target label accessible to a simple classifier. Alain and Bengio used linear classifier probes to study representations across network depth. 10 Hewitt and Liang showed why probe accuracy needs controls for what the probe can learn on its own. 11 Burns and colleagues used unlabeled activations to seek a truth-related direction across several language-model architectures. 12 Here the label is whether a generated program passes its tests, and the probe is a supervised difference-of-means direction. Restricting the classifier makes the read easy to interpret operationally, but it does not establish that the model uses the same direction to determine correctness. Activation steering addresses a different question. Subramani and colleagues extracted latent steering vectors from frozen language models and added them to hidden states during generation. 13 Turner and colleagues showed that activation differences can be added at inference time to influence language-model behaviour. 14 For masked diffusion models, Shnaidman and colleagues studied steering refusal behaviour, 15 and Zhou and colleagues studied attribute-dependent schedules for interventions during denoising. 16 These results motivate testing directions, layers, and intervention timing. They do not imply that a general correctness direction will repair code. The distinction also appears in studies of autoregressive models. Roy and colleagues report that probe-derived directions can detect hallucination-related signals while failing to correct them in their tested settings. 17 Basu and colleagues examine a related gap between internal discrimination and successful intervention in a clinical triage task. 18 Our study examines this question in diffusion code generation, with unit-test labels, confidence controls, perturbations, and direct generation interventions.

sections.heading: 3.1 Tasks, models, and correctness labels
sections.text: We evaluate six diffusion code models: DiffuCoder-7B, Dream-Coder-7B, Stable-DiffCoder-8B, UltraLLaDA-8B, LLaDA2.0-mini, and LLaDA-flash. LLaDA2.0-mini has approximately 1.4B active parameters, whereas LLaDA-flash has approximately 102B total parameters; these counts describe different quantities. All model weights remain frozen. The main programming benchmark is MBPP+, with additional mutation controls on HumanEval+, using the EvalPlus evaluation framework. 19 For a generated attempt, correctness means passing the available unit tests. It does not establish correctness on every possible input. Probing is restricted to mixed problems, for which at least one attempt passes and at least one fails. This allows comparison between attempts at the same problem and reduces the possibility that the probe merely distinguishes easy tasks from difficult ones. It also means the reported read does not describe every task in the benchmark. The family comparison and verification campaign use separate captures. The original DiffuCoder study contains 320 attempts from 64 mixed problems. The fresh 32-step confidence comparison retains 95 attempts from 19 mixed problems; the Qwen2.5-Coder comparison retains 448 attempts from 56 mixed problems. Their generation settings and retained samples are detailed in Appendix B . Differences between captures are not treated as controlled effects of a single parameter.

sections.heading: 3.2 Probes and confidence controls
sections.text: We refer to the response-token-pooled residual-stream activation at a layer as a J-space vector h h . For a collection of labelled attempts, the probe direction is v ∗ = mean ⁡ ( h ∣ pass ) − mean ⁡ ( h ∣ fail ) . v^{*}=\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\mathrm{pass})-\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\mathrm{fail}). The score of an attempt is its projection onto that direction. In the verification campaign, activations are centered within each problem and directions are fitted in five folds grouped by problem. All attempts from a held-out problem remain in the same fold. The original study uses its separately documented held-out-problem protocol; the two analyses should not be conflated. Within-problem area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) measures how often a passing attempt receives a higher score than a failing attempt for the same problem. Scores are averaged across mixed problems. An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to chance ranking, and 1.0 to perfect ranking. We also compare probe scores with model-derived confidence measures, including token entropy and completion log probability. Figure 1 shows the read pipeline. A coding problem Frozen diffusion model Denoises the program in parallel Residual stream at layer L L Pool over response tokens to obtain vector h h Linear probe score = h ⋅ v ∗ \text{score}=h\cdot v^{*} Read: pass or fail Evaluated by AUC Labelled attempts Pass / fail on the tests v ∗ = mean ⁡ ( h ∣ pass ) − mean ⁡ ( h ∣ fail ) v^{*}=\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\text{pass})-\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\text{fail}) Figure 1: Read pipeline. Only the pooled residual-stream vector h h at one layer is read. The probe direction v ∗ v^{*} is built once from labelled attempts (bottom) and then applied to held-out attempts (top). Results are compared with explicit null baselines: shuffled pass/fail labels for probing and random vectors for steering. Layer choice and uncertainty estimation require care. The campaign reports the maximum of the out-of-fold layer curve without a separate layer-selection holdout. Its archived label-shuffle routine keeps fitted scores fixed, and its bootstrap routine does not preserve repeated-cluster multiplicity. We therefore use the reported point estimates descriptively and do not interpret the archived intervals as validated conventional confidence intervals. Appendix B documents these routines and separates them from the original study’s stated protocol.

sections.heading: 3.3 Perturbations and steering
sections.text: Perturbation experiments ask how the read changes when activations are altered. They include random residual displacements and attention-edge ablations. A decline in probe AUC under a perturbation shows that the read depends on the altered representation; it does not by itself show that generation correctness depends on the same feature. We therefore distinguish perturbations of a read from interventions evaluated by generating and testing new code. Li and colleagues shifted selected attention-head activations to improve truthfulness in autoregressive models. 20 Panickssery and colleagues averaged contrastive activation differences and added the resulting direction during generation. 21 These interventions use different targets or activation sites from the correctness edit tested here. Steering experiments add a normalized probe direction to response-token activations, scaled relative to the residual norm. Controls include an untreated baseline and random directions. The campaign also tests interventions restricted to still-masked positions and a learned direction optimized for reference-token log probability. The latter is a surrogate objective, not direct optimization of unit-test success. All eleven campaign conditions run as rows of one generation batch on 30 archived evaluation tasks; exact settings and counts appear in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.1 Correctness is readable beyond surface features
sections.text: Every diffusion model in the family comparison has an observed peak AUC above 0.5. The supplied depth curves peak at approximately 0.68 for Stable-DiffCoder and 0.82 for LLaDA-flash, the endpoints of the range. The curves generally rise beyond the input layers, although they do not share a single shape or peak location (Fig. 2 ). These observations support a readable association with correctness across the tested models. They do not establish a universal correctness feature shared by all model families. Figure 2: Supplied depth curves for six frozen diffusion code models. Correctness is more readable beyond the input layers, with different peaks across models. These reconstructed curves do not uniformly reproduce the originally logged peak readouts (Appendix A ). Final entries are also not uniformly comparable to intermediate blocks; Appendix E examines the additional remeasurements. A probe could otherwise succeed by recognizing surface differences between passing and failing code. The mutation controls reduce this ambiguity by making small semantic changes, such as replacing < with <= , while retaining compilable code and matching mutation kind. The expanded DiffuCoder tests contain 392 MBPP+ mutants and 334 HumanEval+ mutants, with reported AUCs of 0.670 and 0.692. An earlier test on mutations of the model’s own code reports 0.774. These tests constrain a purely stylistic explanation, although they do not exhaust all confounds or establish generalization beyond the tested corpora. Readability also differs from interpretability through output tokens. Projecting the direction through the output embedding yields an explicit error-related vocabulary for the LLaDA2-MoE models, but little such vocabulary for the dense models. That contrast is shown in Appendix A . A direction can discriminate pass/fail labels even when its token-level interpretation is unclear.

sections.heading: 4.2 Confidence provides a competitive readout
sections.text: The fresh DiffuCoder capture gives a probe AUC of 0.842, compared with 0.838 for negative token entropy and 0.798 for the masked-forward confidence score. The matched Qwen2.5-Coder capture gives a probe AUC of 0.677 and a log-probability confidence AUC of 0.703 (Table 1 ). The probe has a small point-estimate advantage in the first comparison and a disadvantage in the second. These observations do not establish that probing provides a consistent advantage over confidence. Table 1: Archived point estimates for the confidence comparisons. Each row uses its own retained mixed-problem cohort. These values do not establish statistical equivalence; uncertainty limitations are described in Appendix B . Model Probe AUC Confidence AUC Confidence measure DiffuCoder-7B 0.842 0.838 Negative token entropy DiffuCoder-7B 0.842 0.798 Masked-forward score Qwen2.5-Coder 0.677 0.703 Completion log probability This comparison changes the interpretation of a successful probe. Above-chance decoding shows that a representation contains a usable signal for the external classifier. It does not show that the signal adds predictive value beyond a simpler quantity already available from the model’s output distribution. Because the archived uncertainty calculation needs correction and the diffusion comparison contains only 19 mixed problems, we leave the size and reliability of any incremental advantage unresolved.

sections.heading: 4.3 A fragile read does not imply fragile generation
sections.text: Random perturbations reduce probe performance, but the behavioural response need not follow the same curve. In the supplied DiffuCoder noise experiment, probe AUC declines while pass@1 remains comparatively stable over the measured behavioural range (Fig. 3 ). The comparison is useful because it prevents an immediate causal interpretation of read degradation: destroying a classifier’s access to a feature need not destroy the model’s ability to solve the task. Figure 3: DiffuCoder probe AUC and generation pass@1 under noise. The supplied curves cover different ranges of noise magnitude. Over the measured behavioural range, the decline in the read does not track a corresponding decline in pass@1. The broader noise and attention-ablation curves are provided in the appendix. The corrected noise study uses five seeds for three models; the other model curves have less complete seed coverage. Pass@1 was not measured for the attention-edge ablation. Its decline in probe performance therefore cannot establish a corresponding decline in generation quality. These distinctions limit how much the perturbation results can explain the steering results.

sections.heading: 4.4 Tested steering procedures do not provide a dependable gain
sections.text: The initial steering experiment compares the probe direction with ten random directions of matched norm. Its reported pass@1 is 0.433 without intervention, 0.429 averaged over random directions, 0.388 when pushed toward the passing direction, and 0.298 when pushed toward the failing direction (Fig. 4 ). The positive probe direction does not improve the observed outcome. The negative direction is more destructive, so the two signs do not behave as symmetric ways to improve and worsen code. Figure 4: Initial DiffuCoder steering experiment. The positive probe direction does not improve the observed pass@1; the negative direction reduces it. The random-direction error bar is the standard deviation across ten directions. The displayed z z values are inherited from the archived analysis. The verification campaign broadens the interventions. The baseline solves 15 of 30 tasks, a global positive probe intervention solves 14, and its negative counterpart solves 5. Restricting the positive probe intervention to masked positions solves 15 tasks. These counts support the narrower conclusion that the tested positive interventions do not deliver a dependable improvement. They do not exclude useful interventions at other layers, strengths, schedules, or task-specific directions. Optimizing a separate direction for reference-token log probability also fails to improve the recorded test outcomes. Its global positive arm passes 5 tasks, compared with 15 for the baseline, and compiles on 9 rather than 26 tasks. The learned direction has cosine similarity 0.108 with the probe direction. This describes the relation between two fitted vectors; it does not prove that either vector captures the causal mechanism of correctness. The full eleven-arm comparison and optimization details are retained in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 5.1 A useful readout need not be a useful intervention
sections.text: The main result is a separation between an external read and the tested attempts at control. A probe can summarize information correlated with successful computation without identifying an operation that supplies missing reasoning. For example, distinguishing a correct loop condition from an incorrect one does not specify which operator to change in an arbitrary failing program. A general pass/fail direction may therefore be less actionable than a representation of a particular repair. Another possibility is that an activation edit is modified or compensated for by later computation. The present experiments do not distinguish that account from the simpler asymmetry that there are more ways to damage working code than to repair broken code. Reports of successful refusal and attribute steering in diffusion models show that activation interventions can work for other targets. 15 , 16 Our negative outcomes concern the correctness directions and intervention settings tested here, rather than activation steering as a whole.

sections.heading: 5.2 Depth and architecture require matched comparisons
sections.text: The additional autoregressive comparisons show readable correctness in some models but not all. They also use different models, training histories, and in some cases different task corpora. The Qwen2.5-Coder comparison is closer to the DiffuCoder setting, but it still does not isolate architecture from training and capture choices. Appendix F retains the cross-model graph while separating these limitations from its descriptive values. The final-layer measurements also resist a simple scaling explanation. The original LLaDA-flash curve prompted a compression hypothesis, but the 7B checks do not show the predicted disappearance of the read. A separate archived Stable-DiffCoder mutant remeasurement also contains a final-layer dip. These observations do not support claiming that such dips occur only at 102B parameters or that a scale threshold has been established. Appendix E gives the tests, normalization differences, and incomplete provenance of the remeasurements.

sections.heading: 5.3 Statistical and reproducibility boundaries
sections.text: The reported results combine historical captures and a verification campaign, not a single frozen benchmark protocol. Mixed-problem filtering changes the population being measured; model and dataset revisions are not consistently pinned; and some capture helpers and activation dumps are absent. The 16-step and 32-step captures differ in retained cohorts, so their observed AUC difference does not isolate the effect of denoising steps. These limitations are relevant to both reproducing the numbers and interpreting differences between conditions. The available campaign code also constrains inferential claims. Fixed-score label permutations differ from refitting the complete probe pipeline under a shuffled-label null, and the archived resampling routine is not a conventional problem-cluster bootstrap. The supplement preserves the original results and explains these issues instead of presenting their calibration as established. A reanalysis with explicit tie handling, correctly weighted problem resampling, and a separate layer-selection evaluation would be needed for stronger claims about significance or equivalence.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: The tested diffusion code models contain representations from which linear probes can read correctness-related information. That observation does not, by itself, provide a method for making the models generate better code. The confidence comparisons offer no consistent point-estimate advantage for the probe, and the tested positive steering interventions provide no dependable gain. The findings motivate more specific interventions that encode a repair rather than a correctness verdict, together with better controlled evaluation of when the relevant information becomes available.

sections.heading: Data availability
sections.text: The accompanying supplementary archive includes the result files used to draw the seven vector graphs, compact campaign summaries, and steering outcome records. Large activation shards, model weights, and a complete frozen benchmark snapshot are not included. File-level provenance and checksums are recorded in the supplementary manifest. Appendix F.1 describes the remaining gaps.

sections.heading: Code availability
sections.text: Supplementary code redraws the supplied graphs and includes the available campaign scripts. The repository address recorded for this project is https://github.com/efficientcomputation/DiffuLM-Steering ; the inspected experiment commit is b38aabc848dae38b10eed39ab948588d06d58d06 . The supplied archive is the versioned companion to this manuscript. Its documentation separates figure regeneration from model reruns and identifies missing dependencies; it does not claim a complete executable reconstruction of all experiments.

sections.heading: Appendix A Model comparison and vocabulary interpretation
sections.text: Probe AUC measures how well passing and failing programs are ranked. Vocabulary decoding asks which output tokens align with an activation direction. These measurements can differ: a correctness direction need not align with words such as “wrong” or “incorrect.” Five of the six depth-curve files flag a mismatch between their reconstructed curves and logged peaks. Table A1 therefore need not match Figure 2 ’s maxima. Final-normalization conventions also differ; Appendix E separates raw and normalized states in the remeasurements. Table A1: Original logged readouts, retained separately from reconstructed depth-curve maxima and later campaign remeasurements. Model Params Logged layer Logged AUC LLaDA-flash 102B L20 0.81 DiffuCoder-7B 7.6B L22 0.78 Dream-Coder-7B 7.6B L28 0.76 LLaDA2.0-mini 1.4B active L14 0.74 UltraLLaDA-8B 8B L27 0.72 Stable-DiffCoder-8B 8.25B L19 0.67 The LLaDA2-MoE models yield stronger enrichment of wrongness terms than the dense coders (Figure A1 ). This is a family-specific vocabulary alignment, not evidence that only one family has a semantic correctness representation. Figure A1: Probe AUC (horizontal axis) and wrongness-word enrichment (vertical axis). All six models have above-chance readouts, but only the LLaDA2-MoE pair strongly enriches explicit “wrong / incorrect” words. The dense coders’ vocabulary enrichment is near the random-direction baseline.

sections.heading: Null distributions.
sections.text: The campaign uses 200 within-problem label permutations against fixed out-of-fold scores, repeating the maximum over layers without refitting directions. The original ledger describes a full-pipeline null; retained perturbation code instead shuffles labels against fixed scores at a preselected layer. The final-layer remeasurements choose the peak before computing its null, without repeating the layer search. Null-standard-deviation scores therefore require protocol-specific interpretation.

sections.heading: Intervals.
sections.text: The archived probe-minus-confidence routine resamples problem identifiers but merges repeats, losing their intended cluster-bootstrap multiplicity. Saved intervals remain for provenance; they are not validated conventional bootstrap intervals. Correction requires resampling paired per-problem AUC differences and addressing layer selection separately. These results do not establish probe–confidence equivalence.

sections.heading: Appendix C Perturbation controls
sections.text: The following controls perturb residual states or attention computation. A decline in probe accuracy alone does not show that generation depends on the measured direction. DiffuCoder, LLaDA-mini, and LLaDA-flash use noise seeds s = 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 s=0,1,2,3,4 , mapped to NumPy seeds 1000000 + s 1000000+s . One random unit direction per example is shared across positions and scaled by the mean token-state norm. This differs from independent noise at each token. Noise records for the other three models remain single-seed; this panel shows the three models with repeated seeds. Figure A2: Correctness readout under noise of relative size m m . Performance generally declines, but the rate and endpoint differ across models. The displayed curves average five noise realizations and do not show a consistent relationship between parameter count and robustness. Attention-edge removal changes the computation producing the readout (Figure A3 ). Generation was not measured in this control. Figure A3: Removing attention edges substantially reduces the read. Most reported per-point null-standard-deviation scores around the sub-chance dips and later increases have | z | < 2 |z|<2 . These single-seed curves do not establish inversion or recovery. Without pass@1 measurements, the effect on generated code is unknown.

sections.heading: Appendix D Steering configuration and complete campaign counts
sections.text: The campaign steering harness intervenes at DiffuCoder block index 18. For a unit direction v v , it adds α ​ r ¯ ​ v \alpha\bar{r}v to selected response positions at every denoising step, where r ¯ \bar{r} is the row’s mean response-token residual norm and α = ± 0.4 \alpha=\pm 0.4 . Global arms affect all response positions; conditional arms affect only positions still containing the mask token. All eleven arms share one generation batch: an untreated baseline, probe directions, random directions, and a learned direction. A fresh random unit direction is sampled per task with NumPy seed 10000 + i 10000+i , where i i is the evaluation-local task index. The archived evaluator specifies 256 new tokens, 32 denoising steps, and temperature 0. The shared batch controls the execution setting, but it does not establish numerical invariance across rows. The original study reports differences between repeated untreated rows in bf16 execution, which motivates caution when interpreting small changes in pass counts. The learned direction starts from the probe and minimizes reference-token negative log probability from a masked-response input while model weights are frozen. The code uses Adam for 25 steps at learning rate 0.005, alternating between two groups of four references. Although the function requests 12 references, only the first eight enter this loop. This objective targets token probability rather than unit-test success; the learned vector is not established as a successful causal correctness direction. The evaluator’s task offset defaults to 120, beyond the 120-task capture used to fit the probe. The archive contains 30 evaluated tasks. Table A3 gives all saved counts, so a reader can compare improvement and degradation directly without interpreting small count differences as general effects. The recorded cosine between the learned and probe directions is 0.108. Together with the degradation under the learned positive arm, this describes the failed optimization attempt rather than identifying a direction that reliably improves correctness. sections.heading: Appendix E Final-layer measurements and the compression hypothesis
sections.text: An apparent final-layer decline can reflect either a change in the representation or a change in what the capture code reports. A transformer block’s raw output and the final normalized state are different quantities. The original depth curves do not record that boundary uniformly, motivating the schematic hypothesis in Figure A4 and the subsequent measurement checks. network depth (layer) → \rightarrow readability of the correctness signal chance final layer(s) built with depth (readable) collapses? output token distribution Figure A4: Schematic of the proposed compression mechanism, not measured data. A late conversion toward output-token directions might reduce a linear probe’s access to correctness information. The DiffuCoder-7B tests below did not support this explanation; they do not establish the mechanism of final-layer changes in every model. The DiffuCoder final-layer battery uses five-fold splits by problem. Logistic regression uses C = 0.05 C=0.05 and at most 2000 iterations. The multilayer perceptron has one 64-unit hidden layer, regularization parameter 0.01, at most 600 iterations, and random seed 0. The vocabulary-subspace test uses the leading 64 right singular vectors of the mean-centered output embedding matrix. The normalization test applies RMSNorm to an already pooled final-block vector; this is not generally equivalent to normalizing each token before pooling. In that capture, the final-block linear AUC is 0.838 against a peak of 0.842; the normalized pooled-vector AUC is 0.816. Splitting the representation by the selected vocabulary subspace gives higher AUC outside it than inside it: 0.829 versus 0.781 at the peak, and 0.811 versus 0.741 at the final block. The tested nonlinear decoder does not yield a higher point estimate than the peak linear probe. These observations do not support the proposed compression mechanism for this DiffuCoder capture; they do not rule out every way another model could reorganize its final states. The LLaDA-flash and Stable remeasurements instead capture final-block token states directly, apply final normalization to each token, and then average. They use compilable reference-code mutants, with passing and failing mutants for each retained base problem. Inputs are truncated to 640 tokens and processed singly. LLaDA-flash records peak AUC 0.8002, raw-final AUC 0.6840, and normalized-final AUC 0.6976. The Stable archive records 0.7301, 0.6086, and 0.6325, respectively. The Stable result is present in runFS.json and its probe log, although the older study ledger says the rerun was unavailable. Its retained script identifies Stable-DiffCoder-8B; immutable checkpoint and dataset revisions are not recorded. It should therefore be read as an archived remeasurement with limited provenance, not a newly reproduced experiment. Its existence also prevents the final-layer dip from being attributed solely to the 102B model or used here to establish a scale threshold.

sections.heading: Appendix F Architecture comparison and artifact provenance
sections.text: A correctness readout is not unique to the diffusion models tested. The archived comparison includes autoregressive Qwen3-Coder and GLM-4.5-Air on SWE-bench-derived rollouts, as well as the later Qwen2.5-Coder campaign on MBPP+. These are not a controlled architecture-only comparison: model families, training, task sources, and retained samples differ. Figure A5: Archived correctness-probe comparison across diffusion and autoregressive models. Each model is compared with its own shuffled-label null. The displayed σ \sigma values describe distances from those model-specific nulls, not a common effect-size scale or calibrated cross-model significance test. Task sources, training, and model identity differ. Qwen2.5-Coder’s campaign probe AUC is 0.677 and its mean token log-probability AUC is 0.703. The comparison shows why a confidence baseline is needed alongside a probe. A readable direction can track a model’s uncertainty without providing additional information or an effective intervention. The archived point estimates and limited uncertainty analysis do not establish that the scores are interchangeable.

sections.heading: F.1 Repository and reproducibility boundary
sections.text: The project repository is identified as https://github.com/efficientcomputation/DiffuLM-Steering . The inspected experiment ancestor is commit b38aabc848dae38b10eed39ab948588d06d58d06 . The accompanying supplementary package contains the retained capture and analysis scripts, result summaries, figure inputs, and documentation for rebuilding the manuscript graphs. Plot rebuilding uses saved measurements and does not rerun model inference. The archive does not provide a complete frozen inference environment or immutable model and dataset revisions. Generation seeds are not set in the retained capture scripts. Some dependencies, including jcode , gradefix , and ladder_subtle2 , are missing from the inspected repository, and some earlier activation dumps are unavailable. The study ledger describes CPU fp32 campaign execution while the retained A/B scripts request bf16; those files alone do not establish the exact executed versions. These gaps limit exact end-to-end reproduction. No new generation experiments or corrected uncertainty estimates were produced for this supplement.

text: The Editor Has Read-Only Access: Correctness Signals in Diffusion Language Models Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: arXiv is now an independent nonprofit! Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.36783v1 [cs.SE] 29 Sep 2026 The Editor Has Read-Only Access: Correctness Signals in Diffusion Language Models Angad Miglani Affiliation: Efficient Computation Inc. Email: angad.miglani@duke.edu Samrath Singh Chadha Affiliation: Efficient Computation Inc. Email: samrath@perseus.so Kevin Li Affiliation: Efficient Computation Inc. Email: kevin.li3@duke.edu Manas Venkata Sai Ravulapalli Affiliation: Efficient Computation Inc. Email: manas@perseus.so Abstract Diffusion language models generate code by repeatedly updating a partially masked sequence. We ask whether their internal activations encode code correctness and whether that information can improve generation. Across six diffusion models, linear probes distinguish passing from failing attempts, with the strongest reads generally appearing beyond the early layers. Controls using small semantic mutations support a connection to correctness rather than surface style alone. In comparisons with model confidence, probe point estimates offer no consistent advantage. Adding a probe-derived direction to the residual stream does not yield a dependable improvement in the tested steering settings, while the opposite direction degrades performance. We distinguish these observations from claims about statistical significance or a general inability to steer. Supplementary methods, archived results, and code document the tested interventions and the limits of their statistical calibration and reproducibility. 1 Introduction A model can contain information that its output does not make useful. For code generation, the distinction is concrete: an activation may help predict whether a program will pass its tests without providing an intervention that repairs the program. Work on language-model self-evaluation shows that models can sometimes estimate whether their answers are correct, although calibration depends on the task and prompting. 1 This motivates a separate question about internal representations: does a readable correctness signal also provide a way to improve generation? Diffusion language models offer a useful setting for this question. Instead of committing to one token at a time, they revise positions in a partially masked sequence over several denoising steps. A correctness-related representation could therefore appear while the program can still change. That possibility does not guarantee control. A probe can correlate with an outcome because it reads the consequences of a computation; moving the representation along the probe direction need not reproduce the computation that caused a correct answer. We study three questions in frozen code models. First, can a linear probe distinguish correct and incorrect attempts at the same programming problem? Second, does it add information beyond the model’s own confidence? Third, can a direction fitted to correctness labels improve the generated code when added to the model’s activations? We compare six diffusion models, run additional checks on DiffuCoder-7B, and use autoregressive models as a comparison rather than as a controlled test of architecture alone. The results separate readability from intervention. Correctness is readable in the tested diffusion models, but the matched confidence comparisons do not show a consistent point-estimate advantage for the probe. The tested steering procedures also do not provide a dependable improvement. These are bounded empirical observations: the captures differ across experiments, some statistical routines need recalibration, and the available code does not constitute a fully frozen reproduction environment. We retain those limits in the main interpretation and give the implementation details in the appendix. 2 Background and related work 2.1 Diffusion and language generation Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues introduced generative modelling through a forward process that gradually corrupts data and a learned reverse process that reconstructs it. 2 Ho and colleagues developed the denoising diffusion probabilistic model formulation that became widely used for continuous data. 3 Language requires a treatment of discrete tokens. Hoogeboom and colleagues developed multinomial diffusion for categorical data, including text. 4 Austin and colleagues studied structured discrete diffusion processes, including transitions involving an absorbing state. 5 Masked language diffusion uses this idea to generate by repeatedly predicting and updating masked positions. Diffusion-LM used continuous word-vector denoising and gradient-based guidance for controllable text generation. 6 For discrete tokens, Sahoo and colleagues developed a masked diffusion language-model objective and sampling recipe. 7 LLaDA demonstrated large-scale language modelling with a masked diffusion objective. 8 DiffuCoder adapted masked diffusion to code and studied how its generation order and reinforcement-learning procedure affect code synthesis. 9 Our experiments use these models as frozen systems. We do not train a new diffusion model or evaluate whether diffusion is generally superior to autoregressive generation. The relevant property is that internal states can be inspected and edited while multiple output positions remain revisable. 2.2 Reading representations and changing behaviour Linear probes test whether a representation makes a target label accessible to a simple classifier. Alain and Bengio used linear classifier probes to study representations across network depth. 10 Hewitt and Liang showed why probe accuracy needs controls for what the probe can learn on its own. 11 Burns and colleagues used unlabeled activations to seek a truth-related direction across several language-model architectures. 12 Here the label is whether a generated program passes its tests, and the probe is a supervised difference-of-means direction. Restricting the classifier makes the read easy to interpret operationally, but it does not establish that the model uses the same direction to determine correctness. Activation steering addresses a different question. Subramani and colleagues extracted latent steering vectors from frozen language models and added them to hidden states during generation. 13 Turner and colleagues showed that activation differences can be added at inference time to influence language-model behaviour. 14 For masked diffusion models, Shnaidman and colleagues studied steering refusal behaviour, 15 and Zhou and colleagues studied attribute-dependent schedules for interventions during denoising. 16 These results motivate testing directions, layers, and intervention timing. They do not imply that a general correctness direction will repair code. The distinction also appears in studies of autoregressive models. Roy and colleagues report that probe-derived directions can detect hallucination-related signals while failing to correct them in their tested settings. 17 Basu and colleagues examine a related gap between internal discrimination and successful intervention in a clinical triage task. 18 Our study examines this question in diffusion code generation, with unit-test labels, confidence controls, perturbations, and direct generation interventions. 3 Methods 3.1 Tasks, models, and correctness labels We evaluate six diffusion code models: DiffuCoder-7B, Dream-Coder-7B, Stable-DiffCoder-8B, UltraLLaDA-8B, LLaDA2.0-mini, and LLaDA-flash. LLaDA2.0-mini has approximately 1.4B active parameters, whereas LLaDA-flash has approximately 102B total parameters; these counts describe different quantities. All model weights remain frozen. The main programming benchmark is MBPP+, with additional mutation controls on HumanEval+, using the EvalPlus evaluation framework. 19 For a generated attempt, correctness means passing the available unit tests. It does not establish correctness on every possible input. Probing is restricted to mixed problems, for which at least one attempt passes and at least one fails. This allows comparison between attempts at the same problem and reduces the possibility that the probe merely distinguishes easy tasks from difficult ones. It also means the reported read does not describe every task in the benchmark. The family comparison and verification campaign use separate captures. The original DiffuCoder study contains 320 attempts from 64 mixed problems. The fresh 32-step confidence comparison retains 95 attempts from 19 mixed problems; the Qwen2.5-Coder comparison retains 448 attempts from 56 mixed problems. Their generation settings and retained samples are detailed in Appendix B . Differences between captures are not treated as controlled effects of a single parameter. 3.2 Probes and confidence controls We refer to the response-token-pooled residual-stream activation at a layer as a J-space vector h h . For a collection of labelled attempts, the probe direction is v ∗ = mean ⁡ ( h ∣ pass ) − mean ⁡ ( h ∣ fail ) . v^{*}=\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\mathrm{pass})-\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\mathrm{fail}). The score of an attempt is its projection onto that direction. In the verification campaign, activations are centered within each problem and directions are fitted in five folds grouped by problem. All attempts from a held-out problem remain in the same fold. The original study uses its separately documented held-out-problem protocol; the two analyses should not be conflated. Within-problem area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) measures how often a passing attempt receives a higher score than a failing attempt for the same problem. Scores are averaged across mixed problems. An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to chance ranking, and 1.0 to perfect ranking. We also compare probe scores with model-derived confidence measures, including token entropy and completion log probability. Figure 1 shows the read pipeline. A coding problem Frozen diffusion model Denoises the program in parallel Residual stream at layer L L Pool over response tokens to obtain vector h h Linear probe score = h ⋅ v ∗ \text{score}=h\cdot v^{*} Read: pass or fail Evaluated by AUC Labelled attempts Pass / fail on the tests v ∗ = mean ⁡ ( h ∣ pass ) − mean ⁡ ( h ∣ fail ) v^{*}=\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\text{pass})-\operatorname{mean}(h\mid\text{fail}) Figure 1: Read pipeline. Only the pooled residual-stream vector h h at one layer is read. The probe direction v ∗ v^{*} is built once from labelled attempts (bottom) and then applied to held-out attempts (top). Results are compared with explicit null baselines: shuffled pass/fail labels for probing and random vectors for steering. Layer choice and uncertainty estimation require care. The campaign reports the maximum of the out-of-fold layer curve without a separate layer-selection holdout. Its archived label-shuffle routine keeps fitted scores fixed, and its bootstrap routine does not preserve repeated-cluster multiplicity. We therefore use the reported point estimates descriptively and do not interpret the archived intervals as validated conventional confidence intervals. Appendix B documents these routines and separates them from the original study’s stated protocol. 3.3 Perturbations and steering Perturbation experiments ask how the read changes when activations are altered. They include random residual displacements and attention-edge ablations. A decline in probe AUC under a perturbation shows that the read depends on the altered representation; it does not by itself show that generation correctness depends on the same feature. We therefore distinguish perturbations of a read from interventions evaluated by generating and testing new code. Li and colleagues shifted selected attention-head activations to improve truthfulness in autoregressive models. 20 Panickssery and colleagues averaged contrastive activation differences and added the resulting direction during generation. 21 These interventions use different targets or activation sites from the correctness edit tested here. Steering experiments add a normalized probe direction to response-token activations, scaled relative to the residual norm. Controls include an untreated baseline and random directions. The campaign also tests interventions restricted to still-masked positions and a learned direction optimized for reference-token log probability. The latter is a surrogate objective, not direct optimization of unit-test success. All eleven campaign conditions run as rows of one generation batch on 30 archived evaluation tasks; exact settings and counts appear in Appendix D . 4 Results 4.1 Correctness is readable beyond surface features Every diffusion model in the family comparison has an observed peak AUC above 0.5. The supplied depth curves peak at approximately 0.68 for Stable-DiffCoder and 0.82 for LLaDA-flash, the endpoints of the range. The curves generally rise beyond the input layers, although they do not share a single shape or peak location (Fig. 2 ). These observations support a readable association with correctness across the tested models. They do not establish a universal correctness feature shared by all model families. Figure 2: Supplied depth curves for six frozen diffusion code models. Correctness is more readable beyond the input layers, with different peaks across models. These reconstructed curves do not uniformly reproduce the originally logged peak readouts (Appendix A ). Final entries are also not uniformly comparable to intermediate blocks; Appendix E examines the additional remeasurements. A probe could otherwise succeed by recognizing surface differences between passing and failing code. The mutation controls reduce this ambiguity by making small semantic changes, such as replacing < with <= , while retaining compilable code and matching mutation kind. The expanded DiffuCoder tests contain 392 MBPP+ mutants and 334 HumanEval+ mutants, with reported AUCs of 0.670 and 0.692. An earlier test on mutations of the model’s own code reports 0.774. These tests constrain a purely stylistic explanation, although they do not exhaust all confounds or establish generalization beyond the tested corpora. Readability also differs from interpretability through output tokens. Projecting the direction through the output embedding yields an explicit error-related vocabulary for the LLaDA2-MoE models, but little such vocabulary for the dense models. That contrast is shown in Appendix A . A direction can discriminate pass/fail labels even when its token-level interpretation is unclear. 4.2 Confidence provides a competitive readout The fresh DiffuCoder capture gives a probe AUC of 0.842, compared with 0.838 for negative token entropy and 0.798 for the masked-forward confidence score. The matched Qwen2.5-Coder capture gives a probe AUC of 0.677 and a log-probability confidence AUC of 0.703 (Table 1 ). The probe has a small point-estimate advantage in the first comparison and a disadvantage in the second. These observations do not establish that probing provides a consistent advantage over confidence. Table 1: Archived point estimates for the confidence comparisons. Each row uses its own retained mixed-problem cohort. These values do not establish statistical equivalence; uncertainty limitations are described in Appendix B . Model Probe AUC Confidence AUC Confidence measure DiffuCoder-7B 0.842 0.838 Negative token entropy DiffuCoder-7B 0.842 0.798 Masked-forward score Qwen2.5-Coder 0.677 0.703 Completion log probability This comparison changes the interpretation of a successful probe. Above-chance decoding shows that a representation contains a usable signal for the external classifier. It does not show that the signal adds predictive value beyond a simpler quantity already available from the model’s output distribution. Because the archived uncertainty calculation needs correction and the diffusion comparison contains only 19 mixed problems, we leave the size and reliability of any incremental advantage unresolved. 4.3 A fragile read does not imply fragile generation Random perturbations reduce probe performance, but the behavioural response need not follow the same curve. In the supplied DiffuCoder noise experiment, probe AUC declines while pass@1 remains comparatively stable over the measured behavioural range (Fig. 3 ). The comparison is useful because it prevents an immediate causal interpretation of read degradation: destroying a classifier’s access to a feature need not destroy the model’s ability to solve the task. Figure 3: DiffuCoder probe AUC and generation pass@1 under noise. The supplied curves cover different ranges of noise magnitude. Over the measured behavioural range, the decline in the read does not track a corresponding decline in pass@1. The broader noise and attention-ablation curves are provided in the appendix. The corrected noise study uses five seeds for three models; the other model curves have less complete seed coverage. Pass@1 was not measured for the attention-edge ablation. Its decline in probe performance therefore cannot establish a corresponding decline in generation quality. These distinctions limit how much the perturbation results can explain the steering results. 4.4 Tested steering procedures do not provide a dependable gain The initial steering experiment compares the probe direction with ten random directions of matched norm. Its reported pass@1 is 0.433 without intervention, 0.429 averaged over random directions, 0.388 when pushed toward the passing direction, and 0.298 when pushed toward the failing direction (Fig. 4 ). The positive probe direction does not improve the observed outcome. The negative direction is more destructive, so the two signs do not behave as symmetric ways to improve and worsen code. Figure 4: Initial DiffuCoder steering experiment. The positive probe direction does not improve the observed pass@1; the negative direction reduces it. The random-direction error bar is the standard deviation across ten directions. The displayed z z values are inherited from the archived analysis. The verification campaign broadens the interventions. The baseline solves 15 of 30 tasks, a global positive probe intervention solves 14, and its negative counterpart solves 5. Restricting the positive probe intervention to masked positions solves 15 tasks. These counts support the narrower conclusion that the tested positive interventions do not deliver a dependable improvement. They do not exclude useful interventions at other layers, strengths, schedules, or task-specific directions. Optimizing a separate direction for reference-token log probability also fails to improve the recorded test outcomes. Its global positive arm passes 5 tasks, compared with 15 for the baseline, and compiles on 9 rather than 26 tasks. The learned direction has cosine similarity 0.108 with the probe direction. This describes the relation between two fitted vectors; it does not prove that either vector captures the causal mechanism of correctness. The full eleven-arm comparison and optimization details are retained in Appendix D . 5 Discussion and limitations 5.1 A useful readout need not be a useful intervention The main result is a separation between an external read and the tested attempts at control. A probe can summarize information correlated with successful computation without identifying an operation that supplies missing reasoning. For example, distinguishing a correct loop condition from an incorrect one does not specify which operator to change in an arbitrary failing program. A general pass/fail direction may therefore be less actionable than a representation of a particular repair. Another possibility is that an activation edit is modified or compensated for by later computation. The present experiments do not distinguish that account from the simpler asymmetry that there are more ways to damage working code than to repair broken code. Reports of successful refusal and attribute steering in diffusion models show that activation interventions can work for other targets. 15 , 16 Our negative outcomes concern the correctness directions and intervention settings tested here, rather than activation steering as a whole. 5.2 Depth and architecture require matched comparisons The additional autoregressive comparisons show readable correctness in some models but not all. They also use different models, training histories, and in some cases different task corpora. The Qwen2.5-Coder comparison is closer to the DiffuCoder setting, but it still does not isolate architecture from training and capture choices. Appendix F retains the cross-model graph while separating these limitations from its descriptive values. The final-layer measurements also resist a simple scaling explanation. The original LLaDA-flash curve prompted a compression hypothesis, but the 7B checks do not show the predicted disappearance of the read. A separate archived Stable-DiffCoder mutant remeasurement also contains a final-layer dip. These observations do not support claiming that such dips occur only at 102B parameters or that a scale threshold has been established. Appendix E gives the tests, normalization differences, and incomplete provenance of the remeasurements. 5.3 Statistical and reproducibility boundaries The reported results combine historical captures and a verification campaign, not a single frozen benchmark protocol. Mixed-problem filtering changes the population being measured; model and dataset revisions are not consistently pinned; and some capture helpers and activation dumps are absent. The 16-step and 32-step captures differ in retained cohorts, so their observed AUC difference does not isolate the effect of denoising steps. These limitations are relevant to both reproducing the numbers and interpreting differences between conditions. The available campaign code also constrains inferential claims. Fixed-score label permutations differ from refitting the complete probe pipeline under a shuffled-label null, and the archived resampling routine is not a conventional problem-cluster bootstrap. The supplement preserves the original results and explains these issues instead of presenting their calibration as established. A reanalysis with explicit tie handling, correctly weighted problem resampling, and a separate layer-selection evaluation would be needed for stronger claims about significance or equivalence. 6 Conclusion The tested diffusion code models contain representations from which linear probes can read correctness-related information. That observation does not, by itself, provide a method for making the models generate better code. The confidence comparisons offer no consistent point-estimate advantage for the probe, and the tested positive steering interventions provide no dependable gain. The findings motivate more specific interventions that encode a repair rather than a correctness verdict, together with better controlled evaluation of when the relevant information becomes available. Data availability The accompanying supplementary archive includes the result files used to draw the seven vector graphs, compact campaign summaries, and steering outcome records. Large activation shards, model weights, and a complete frozen benchmark snapshot are not included. File-level provenance and checksums are recorded in the supplementary manifest. Appendix F.1 describes the remaining gaps. Code availability Supplementary code redraws the supplied graphs and includes the available campaign scripts. The repository address recorded for this project is https://github.com/efficientcomputation/DiffuLM-Steering ; the inspected experiment commit is b38aabc848dae38b10eed39ab948588d06d58d06 . The supplied archive is the versioned companion to this manuscript. Its documentation separates figure regeneration from model reruns and identifies missing dependencies; it does not claim a complete executable reconstruction of all experiments. Appendix A Model comparison and vocabulary interpretation Probe AUC measures how well passing and failing programs are ranked. Vocabulary decoding asks which output tokens align with an activation direction. These measurements can differ: a correctness direction need not align with words such as “wrong” or “incorrect.” Five of the six depth-curve files flag a mismatch between their reconstructed curves and logged peaks. Table A1 therefore need not match Figure 2 ’s maxima. Final-normalization conventions also differ; Appendix E separates raw and normalized states in the remeasurements. Table A1: Original logged readouts, retained separately from reconstructed depth-curve maxima and later campaign remeasurements. Model Params Logged layer Logged AUC LLaDA-flash 102B L20 0.81 DiffuCoder-7B 7.6B L22 0.78 Dream-Coder-7B 7.6B L28 0.76 LLaDA2.0-mini 1.4B active L14 0.74 UltraLLaDA-8B 8B L27 0.72 Stable-DiffCoder-8B 8.25B L19 0.67 The LLaDA2-MoE models yield stronger enrichment of wrongness terms than the dense coders (Figure A1 ). This is a family-specific vocabulary alignment, not evidence that only one family has a semantic correctness representation. Figure A1: Probe AUC (horizontal axis) and wrongness-word enrichment (vertical axis). All six models have above-chance readouts, but only the LLaDA2-MoE pair strongly enriches explicit “wrong / incorrect” words. The dense coders’ vocabulary enrichment is near the random-direction baseline. Appendix B Capture protocol, scoring, and uncertainty Table A2 counts retained examples. Mixed problems contain passing and failing attempts; evaluation ranks alternatives to the same task, not the full benchmark. The family comparison and campaign use different captures. Table A2: Archived verification cohorts. Counts describe retained examples, not the full benchmark size. Cohort Problems Examples DiffuCoder, 32 denoising steps 19 95 DiffuCoder, 16 denoising steps 54 324 Qwen2.5-Coder, generated attempts 56 448 DiffuCoder, MBPP+ mutants 52 392 DiffuCoder, HumanEval+ mutants 44 334 LLaDA-flash / Stable remeasurement 53 399 each Logs record 120 tasks with five attempts each for 32-step DiffuCoder, and 180 with eight attempts each for Qwen2.5-Coder. Analysis uses DiffuCoder’s last-step response-token mean and Qwen’s completion-token mean. The 16-step and 32-step cohorts differ, so their AUCs do not isolate a step-count effect. Activations are centered within problem. Five folds are assigned by problem using NumPy seed 0; attempts from the same problem never cross folds. The normalized difference between passing and failing training activations defines each fold’s direction. AUCs of held-out projections are averaged equally across mixed problems. The implementation uses sorted ranks without explicit tie averaging. The maximum of the out-of-fold curve selects the reported layer, without a separate layer-selection holdout. Diffusion confidence controls use mean visible-token log probability, negative mean visible-token entropy, and mean completion log probability with response positions masked. Diffusion logits at i i score token i i ; autoregressive logits score the following token. Visible and masked passes condition on different information. Null distributions. The campaign uses 200 within-problem label permutations against fixed out-of-fold scores, repeating the maximum over layers without refitting directions. The original ledger describes a full-pipeline null; retained perturbation code instead shuffles labels against fixed scores at a preselected layer. The final-layer remeasurements choose the peak before computing its null, without repeating the layer search. Null-standard-deviation scores therefore require protocol-specific interpretation. Intervals. The archived probe-minus-confidence routine resamples problem identifiers but merges repeats, losing their intended cluster-bootstrap multiplicity. Saved intervals remain for provenance; they are not validated conventional bootstrap intervals. Correction requires resampling paired per-problem AUC differences and addressing layer selection separately. These results do not establish probe–confidence equivalence. Appendix C Perturbation controls The following controls perturb residual states or attention computation. A decline in probe accuracy alone does not show that generation depends on the measured direction. DiffuCoder, LLaDA-mini, and LLaDA-flash use noise seeds s = 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 s=0,1,2,3,4 , mapped to NumPy seeds 1000000 + s 1000000+s . One random unit direction per example is shared across positions and scaled by the mean token-state norm. This differs from independent noise at each token. Noise records for the other three models remain single-seed; this panel shows the three models with repeated seeds. Figure A2: Correctness readout under noise of relative size m m . Performance generally declines, but the rate and endpoint differ across models. The displayed curves average five noise realizations and do not show a consistent relationship between parameter count and robustness. Attention-edge removal changes the computation producing the readout (Figure A3 ). Generation was not measured in this control. Figure A3: Removing attention edges substantially reduces the read. Most reported per-point null-standard-deviation scores around the sub-chance dips and later increases have | z | < 2 |z|<2 . These single-seed curves do not establish inversion or recovery. Without pass@1 measurements, the effect on generated code is unknown. The original study reports differences between repeated untreated rows in bf16 execution, which motivates caution when interpreting small changes in pass counts. The learned direction starts from the probe and minimizes reference-token negative log probability from a masked-response input while model weights are frozen. The code uses Adam for 25 steps at learning rate 0.005, alternating between two groups of four references. Although the function requests 12 references, only the first eight enter this loop. Appendix E Final-layer measurements and the compression hypothesis An apparent final-layer decline can reflect either a change in the representation or a change in what the capture code reports. A transformer block’s raw output and the final normalized state are different quantities. The original depth curves do not record that boundary uniformly, motivating the schematic hypothesis in Figure A4 and the subsequent measurement checks. network depth (layer) → \rightarrow readability of the correctness signal chance final layer(s) built with depth (readable) collapses? output token distribution Figure A4: Schematic of the proposed compression mechanism, not measured data. A late conversion toward output-token directions might reduce a linear probe’s access to correctness information. The DiffuCoder-7B tests below did not support this explanation; they do not establish the mechanism of final-layer changes in every model. The DiffuCoder final-layer battery uses five-fold splits by problem. Logistic regression uses C = 0.05 C=0.05 and at most 2000 iterations. The multilayer perceptron has one 64-unit hidden layer, regularization parameter 0.01, at most 600 iterations, and random seed 0. The vocabulary-subspace test uses the leading 64 right singular vectors of the mean-centered output embedding matrix. The normalization test applies RMSNorm to an already pooled final-block vector; this is not generally equivalent to normalizing each token before pooling. In that capture, the final-block linear AUC is 0.838 against a peak of 0.842; the normalized pooled-vector AUC is 0.816. Splitting the representation by the selected vocabulary subspace gives higher AUC outside it than inside it: 0.829 versus 0.781 at the peak, and 0.811 versus 0.741 at the final block. The tested nonlinear decoder does not yield a higher point estimate than the peak linear probe. These observations do not support the proposed compression mechanism for this DiffuCoder capture; they do not rule out every way another model could reorganize its final states. The LLaDA-flash and Stable remeasurements instead capture final-block token states directly, apply final normalization to each token, and then average. They use compilable reference-code mutants, with passing and failing mutants for each retained base problem. Inputs are truncated to 640 tokens and processed singly. LLaDA-flash records peak AUC 0.8002, raw-final AUC 0.6840, and normalized-final AUC 0.6976. The Stable archive records 0.7301, 0.6086, and 0.6325, respectively. The Stable result is present in runFS.json and its probe log, although the older study ledger says the rerun was unavailable. Its retained script identifies Stable-DiffCoder-8B; immutable checkpoint and dataset revisions are not recorded. It should therefore be read as an archived remeasurement with limited provenance, not a newly reproduced experiment. Its existence also prevents the final-layer dip from being attributed solely to the 102B model or used here to establish a scale threshold. F.1 Repository and reproducibility boundary The project repository is identified as https://github.com/efficientcomputation/DiffuLM-Steering . The inspected experiment ancestor is commit b38aabc848dae38b10eed39ab948588d06d58d06 . The accompanying supplementary package contains the retained capture and analysis scripts, result summaries, figure inputs, and documentation for rebuilding the manuscript graphs. Plot rebuilding uses saved measurements and does not rerun model inference. The archive does not provide a complete frozen inference environment or immutable model and dataset revisions. Generation seeds are not set in the retained capture scripts. Some dependencies, including jcode , gradefix , and ladder_subtle2 , are missing from the inspected repository, and some earlier activation dumps are unavailable. The study ledger describes CPU fp32 campaign execution while the retained A/B scripts request bf16; those files alone do not establish the exact executed versions. These gaps limit exact end-to-end reproduction. No new generation experiments or corrected uncertainty estimates were produced for this supplement.
